TfOH-Catalyzed Phosphinylation of 2,3-Allenols into
γ‑Ketophosphine Oxides
Runmin Zhao, Xianhua Huang, Minning Wang, Shanshan Hu, Yuxing Gao, * Pengxiang Xu, *
and Yufen Zhao
Cite This: J. Org. Chem. 2020, 85, 8185 −8195 Read Online
ACCESS Metrics & More Article Recommendations *sı Supporting Information
ABSTRACT: The ﬁrst facile and e ﬃcient acid-catalyzed direct
coupling of a wide range of unprotected 2,3-allenols with
arylphosphine oxides was developed, o ﬀering a general, one-step
approach for the synthesis of structurally diverse γ-ketophosphine
oxides accompanied by concurrent C P/CO bond formation
with remarkable functional group tolerance and complete atom-
economy under metal- and additive-free conditions. Mechanistic
studies showed that this transformation involved a rearrangement and a phospha-Michael reaction.
O
rganophosphorus compounds have found widespread
applications in organic synthesis, medicinal chemistry,
agricultural chemistry, and materials science.
1 Among them, γ-
ketophosphine oxides have attracted extensive attention in
organic and medicinal chemistry over the past few decades due
to their unique structural features and diverse intriguing
biological properties. 2 Thus, intense research interests have
been directed toward developing synthetic approaches to such
promising frameworks. The majority of these methods involve
the conjugate addition of phosphorus nucleophiles to α,β-
unsaturated carbonyl compounds, namely, the phospha-
Michael reaction ( Scheme 1 a), which su ﬀers from the use of
a large amount of bases 3 or complex N-heterocyclic carbene 4
as the catalyst and limited substrate scope. To address these
disadvantages, a few synthetic methods have emerged in recent
years. In 2014, the Ag-promoted radical phosphinylation of
α,α-diaryl allylic alcohols with arylphosphine oxides for the
preparation of γ-ketophosphine oxides was revealed, which is
usually plagued by the use of a large amount of noble Ag salts
(Scheme 1 b, eq 1).
5 In 2017, our group established a
Zn(OTf)2-catalyzed direct coupling of propargylic alcohols
with P(O)H compounds to access γ-ketophosphine oxides in
the presence of Ph 2P(O)OH ( Scheme 1 c), but their general
use poses severe limitations due to environmentally unfriendly
metal catalyst and the limited substrate scope. 6 Very recently,
Zhang’s group developed Eosin Y-catalyzed phosphinylation of
allylic alcohols assisted by blue LEDs ( Scheme 1 b, eq 2). 7
Although these synthetic methods have proven to be e ﬃcient,
the development of new catalytic systems with di ﬀerent
synthons for the synthesis of diverse γ-ketophosphine oxides
for biological screening under metal- and additive-free
conditions is still of great signi ﬁcance.
Over the past several years, 2,3-allenols and their derivatives
have been employed as structurally diverse and fascinating
building blocks for the construction of C C and C X
bonds,8 as well as for the preparation of a wide range of
valuable molecular frames in modern organic synthesis, such as

dihydrofurans,9 lactams,10 enynes,11 2-pyrrolines,12 carba-
zoles,13 and furanones. 14 Inspired by these precedents and
our recent work on C P bond formation, 15 we disclosed the
ﬁrst example of a single-step and selective synthesis of
structurally diverse γ-ketophosphine oxide frameworks via a
simple and e ﬃcient Brønsted acid-catalyzed direct phosphiny-
lation of unprotected 2,3-allenols under metal-free and
additive-free conditions with remarkable functional group
tolerance, high regioselectivity, complete atom-economy, and
moderate to excellent yields ( Scheme 1 d). This metal-free
strategy provided facile and rapid access to various novel γ-
ketophosphine oxides, which were not easily accessible by the
known methods, along with the formation of new C P and
CO bonds.
Our initial investigation focused on the C P coupling
reaction of 1-phenyl-2,3-butadien-1-ol 1a with diphenylphos-
phine oxide 2a as summarized in Table 1 . Gratifyingly,
preliminary attempts using 20 mol % of Zn(OTf)
2 as the
catalyst in 1,2-dichloroethane (DCE) at 100 °C for 24 h under
an argon atmosphere resulted in clean formation of anticipated
product 3a in a high yield of 81% ( Table 1 , entry 1).
Encouraged by this promising result, we turned to screen the
eﬀect of other solvents such as toluene, dioxane, and
tetrahydrofuran (THF) and found that THF was the optimal
solvent for this reaction and could enhance the yield up to 90%
(Table 1 , entries 1 −4). Subsequently, the performance of a
series of catalysts was examined. Substituting Zn(OTf)
2 for
Al(OTf)3, NHTf 2, B(PhF 5)3,o rB F 3·Et2O as Lewis acid gave
rise to a decrease of the yield of 3a (entries 5−8). A screening
of various Brønsted acids including TEA, H 2SO4, and TfOH as
the catalyst was then carried out, with the ﬁnding that the
formation of 3a was observed in all cases and simple TfOH
gave the best result for this reaction, providing the desired
product 3a in an excellent yield of 92% (entries 9 −11).
Conversely, no product was detected in the absence of TfOH,
and only starting materials were recovered (entry 12). To our
delight, increasing the loading of TfOH to 30 mol % could
enhance the yield of 3a up to 95% (entry 13). Yet, further
increasing the TfOH loading led to a slight decrease in yield
(entry 14). Considering that THF may form a complex with
the TfOH and weaken the acidity of the TfOH, we retested the
eﬀect of various solvents such as toluene, DCM, and DCE by
using 10 mol % TfOH, but none of these gave better results
(entries 15 −17), indicating that THF was the optimal solvent
for the reaction. Finally, the e ﬀect of temperature was
evaluated, and we found that increasing or decreasing the
temperature from 100 °C resulted in the yield reduction
(entries 18 and 19).
With the optimized conditions in hand (footnote a, Table
2), the substrate scope of the phosphinylation of various
structurally and electronically modulated 2,3-allenols with
diphenylphosphine oxide 2a was explored, and the results are
summarized in Table 2 . In the beginning, 13 derivatives ( 1b−

1n)o f 1a with di ﬀerent electron-donating or -withdrawing
groups on the phenyl ring were tested. Various substituents
such as Me, Ph, OMe, SMe, F, Cl, Br, CF
3,C O2Me, NO2, and
CN were all well tolerated for this method and their electronic
nature was not evident for this transformation. The bulky
naphthyl-derived 2,3-allenol underwent the coupling to a ﬀord
the desired product 3o in 95% yield. In addition, substrates
incorporating heterocyclic groups such as furyl ( 1p), thienyl
(1q), or benzothienyl ( 1s) were also tolerated well. Subjecting
pyridyl-substituted 2,3-allenol 1r to the standard reaction
conditions did not a ﬀord the targeted product, yet with 1.3
equiv of TfOH at 90 °C, the reaction could give the expected
product 3r in 42% yield. To our delight, aliphatic 2,3-allenols
1t−1v could also successfully be applied to this coupling.
Interestingly, 1w and 1x having double bond and triple bond at
C1 position also worked under the standard conditions. In
addition to secondary 2,3-allenols, tertiary 2,3-allenols were
also successfully engaged in this reaction, producing the
corresponding products 3y−3aa in good to excellent yields of
79−99%. It should be noted that tertiary 2,3-allenols such as
1,1-diphenyl-buta-2,3-dien-1-ol with two phenyls at the C1
position failed to a ﬀord the expected product under the
optimized conditions, which might be attributed to steric
hindrance. After investigating the reactivity of 1-substituted
2,3-allenols, we turned our attention to the use of 1,2-
disubstituted 2,3-allenols. When a methyl group was
introduced at C2 position, 1ab could be converted into the
desired product 3ab in high total yield along with a
diastereomeric ratio of 65:35. Next, the in ﬂuence of
substituents at the terminal position of the allene moiety was
surveyed. 4,4-Diphenyl-substituted 2,3-allenol 1ac could also
participate in the reaction to generate the corresponding
product 3ac in 56% yield. However, when 4-phenyl-substituted
2,3-allenol 1ad was employed, an unsatisfactory yield of 25%
was obtained. It is noteworthy that 2,3-allenols with an alkyl
group at their C4 position were also compatible with this
protocol and gave the related products 3ae−3ai in moderate to
good yields. Fortunately, the product 3e was recrystallized
from acetone as colorless crystals by slow evaporation at room
temperature, and the molecular structure of 3e was con ﬁrmed
by X-ray di ﬀraction analysis (see the Supporting Information
for detailed X-ray crystallography data).
16 The result clearly
showed the phosphoryl moiety was preferentially installed at
the C1-position of 2,3-allenols in the present coupling reaction.
To gain more insight into the versatility of the reaction,
some other P(O)H substrates were also evaluated. As shown in
Table 3 , apart from 2a, other diarylphosphine oxides such as
2b, 2c, and 2d were all suitable reaction partners and a ﬀorded
the desired products 3aj−3al in excellent yields (94% −99%).
Moreover, dibutylphosphine oxide 2e could also be success-
fully converted into the corresponding product 3am in 67%
yield by increasing the temperature to 140 °C. Nevertheless,
ethyl phenylphosphinate 2f only provided the target product
3an in a lower yield of 12%. Notably, H-phosphonates like
diethyl phosphonate were almost inert in the present catalytic
system, probably due to the electronic properties of P(O)H
compounds. To examine the stereochemistry of this reaction,
optically pure (S)- tert-butyl(phenyl)phosphine oxide (99% ee)
2h was used as the substrate under the standard reaction
conditions, but the corresponding product 3ap was acquired in
a racemic form, which was proposed with the low
diastereocontrol (3.4:1 dr).
To demonstrate the practical utility of this method, a gram-
scale reaction of 1a (1.46 g, 10 mmol) with 2a (2.43 g, 12
mmol) was conducted to a ﬀord the expected product 3a (3.46
g) in 99% yield ( Scheme 2a), indicating that the reaction could
be e ﬀectively scaled up without decreasing the yields.
Moreover, the products could be easily transformed to other
derivatives.
5,17 For example, 3a could react with HBr to
produce a useful α-bromocarbonyl compound 4 (Scheme 2b).
To gain preliminary insight into the reaction mechanism,
several control experiments were performed ( Scheme 3 ).
Treatment of 1a under the standard reaction conditions
without 2a, as expected, produced enone 5 in 51% yield. Yet,
no product 5 was observed in the absence of TfOH ( Scheme
3a). Further treatment of enone 5 with 2a could give the
targeted product 3a in 96% yield ( Scheme 3 b), showing that
enone 5 should be the key intermediate in this transformation.
On the basis of the experimental results and related
literature reports, 18−20 we proposed a tentative mechanism
for this transformation ( Scheme 4). Initially, the elimination of
the hydroxyl group in the 2,3-allenol moiety easily occurred
with the aid of TfOH to produce the carbenium ion A,
followed by electron transfer of A to a ﬀord the corresponding

vinyl cation B.18b Ensuing nucleophilic attack of water led to
an enol intermediate C, which immediately isomerizes to form
the key enone intermediate D.18 Finally, the intermolecular
phospha-Michael addition of the phosphorus nucleophile 2′
(tautomerized from 219)t o D resulted in the formation of an
enol intermediate E with the assistance of TfOH, 20 followed by
enol−keto tautomerism of E to generate the desired product 3.
In conclusion, we have developed the ﬁrst facile and e ﬃcient
TfOH-catalyzed direct phosphinylation of a wide range of 2,3-
allenols with H-phosphine oxides, a ﬀording a rapid and
powerful tool to a structurally diverse array of γ-ketophosphine
oxides along with concurrent new C O and C P bond
formation. Importantly, the present method avoids metals and
other additives, and various valuable γ-ketophosphine oxide
moieties could be easily obtained through a simple one-step
process. Mechanistic investigations showed that this trans-
formation involved a rearrangement to the enone intermediate,
followed by the phospha-Michael reaction. In addition, the use
of readily available TfOH as the catalyst, operational simplicity,
remarkable functional group tolerance, excellent regioselectiv-
ity, and complete atom economy mean that this method will
open a new avenue to potential biologically active γ-
ketophosphine oxide and ﬁnd widespread applications in
synthetic chemistry and medicinal chemistry.
■ EXPERIMENTAL SECTION
General Information. Unless otherwise stated, all reactions were
carried out under dry argon. Substrates 1a−1aa,21 1ab,12 1ac,221ad,23
1ae−1ai,24 2c−2d,25 2e,26 and 2h27 were prepared according to the
known reference. Other reagents were obtained from commercial
suppliers and used without further puri ﬁcation. All the heating
experiments were performed in an oil bath.
1H, 13C, and 31P NMR
spectra were recorded on a Bruker AV500 spectrometer using
tetramethylsilane (TMS) in CDCl
3 as the internal standard. NMR
chemical shifts were determined relative to CDCl 3 as the internal
reference ( δH = 7.26 ppm, δC = 77.16 ppm). NMR data are
represented as follows: chemical shift, multiplicity (s = singlet, d =
doublet, t = triplet, q = quartet, m = multiplet), coupling constants in
Hertz (Hz), integration. HRMS spectra of all products were recorded
on a Waters Micromass LCT Premier TOF-MS apparatus. Infrared
spectra were recorded on a Nicolet Avatar 330 spectrometer. Melting
points were recorded on a MP120 digital melting-point apparatus.
The products were puri ﬁed by column chromatography on silica gel
300−400 mesh. Flash column chromatography puri ﬁcation was
carried out by a gradient elution method using ethyl acetate (EA)
in light petroleum ether (PE).
General Procedure for the Synthesis of γ-Ketophosphine Oxides
(3aa−3ap). To a Schlenk tube equipped with a magnetic stir bar was
added 2,3-allenols (0.4 mmol), H-phosphine oxides (0.48 mmol), and
TfOH (0.12 mmol) in THF (2 mL) under argon, and the mixture was
kept stirring at 100 °C in an oil bath for 24 h. The resulting mixture
was cooled down to room temperature and puri ﬁed by ﬂash
chromatography (petroleum ether/ethyl acetate) to a ﬀord the
corresponding products.
